Some of my own header investigation for the `2025-10-03` update:
- `memory.h`: Has unnecessary `safe_refcount.h` include, addressed in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111066. Otherwise, it's often a short path to `typedefs.h` which makes it score high.
- `char_utils.h`: Has unnecessary `<iterator>` include. It's the shortest path from `ustring.h` to `typedefs.h`, which is probably what makes it score high. Addressed in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111223
- `hash_set.h`: Looks minimal to me, investigate includees and includers instead.
- `list.h`: Looks minimal to me, investigate includees and includers instead.
- `a_hash_map.h`: Has unnecessary `hash_map.h` include, addressed in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111221. Otherwise minimal, investigate includees and includers instead.
- `hashfuncs.h`: Largely addressed by https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/106434.
- `rw_lock.h`: Unnecessarily included in `object.h`. It's now included in `class_db.h`, so will probably re-appear, but https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111254 is a start.

`canvas_item.h` includes `scene/resources/font.h` solely to get default values from `Font::DEFAULT_FONT_SIZE` and also `TextServer` indirectly. Of course, most users of `CanvasItem` don't necessarily use `CanvasItem`'s text rendering functions, so this is a waste.

Moving them to a separate `text_defs.h` header (like `math_defs.h`) might be a good idea. This would also benefit `tree.h`, which is also including `scene/resources/text_paragraph.h` just to get access to `TextServer`'s enums.

> `canvas_item.h` includes `scene/resources/font.h` solely to get default values from `Font::DEFAULT_FONT_SIZE` and also `TextServer` indirectly. Of course, most users of `CanvasItem` don't necessarily use `CanvasItem`'s text rendering functions, so this is a waste.
> 
> Moving them to a separate `text_defs.h` header (like `math_defs.h`) might be a good idea. This would also benefit `tree.h`, which is also including `scene/resources/text_paragraph.h` just to get access to `TextServer`'s enums.

Agreed. This is something we need to do as well for several other headers, e.g. `variant.h`, `rendering_server.h` and `display_server.h`.

> Moving them to a separate `text_defs.h` header (like `math_defs.h`) might be a good idea. This would also benefit `tree.h`, which is also including `scene/resources/text_paragraph.h` just to get access to `TextServer`'s enums.

On the second thought, this would inevitably become a *very* noisy commit, since there's a lot of existing code that uses code like `TextServer::<enum value>`.

I've thought about adding `typedef`s in `TextServer` to redirect old usage to the enums defined in the new header, but this would require users of the enums to always specify the enum's type name in order to use them.

Another solution would be to have a `text_defs.inc` that's pasted into `text_defs.h` wrapped in a namespace, and also into `text_server.h`, but this would make it impossible to convert one into another implicitly, resulting in a lot of type-casts that need to be added retroactively.

I think I'll hold off from this one for now.

Putting up some of my other investigations here as well:
* `cowdata.h`: Most of the implementation can be split into a type-erased `CowMemory` base class. (dealing with `void *` plus a specified size) Functions like `push_back` and `_insert` are already decently complex and I doubt if they're actually inlined by the compiler, so the performance impact would be minimal. The templated `CowData` then acts as a type-safe wrapper to `CowMemory`. This should reduce the amount of redundant work by the compiler.
  * Might still want to run some benchmarks afterwards, though.
* `vector.h`: Something similar to `CowData` above could also work for `Vector` here, but `Vector` is already mostly a wrapper to `CowData` anyway so it's likely not going to help much. I'd say it's as minimal as it can be. Look elsewhere.
* `vector3.h`: The error check in `Vector3::get_any_perpendicular()` *should* be wrapped with `#ifdef MATH_CHECKS` to be consistent with other math classes, and this would allow the `error_macros.h` include to be conditionally dropped as well. This does change the engine's behavior outside of debug builds, however, so it might be better to keep the branch hidden inside the error macro.
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/06827c91c6ee98068a48c66be0cc067ebb434a2f/core/math/vector3.h#L368-L376
* `ustring.h`: Not much to improve here directly, but the `cowdata.h` include is technically unnecessary here. (already included by `vector.h`) I'd probably keep it though, as it's used directly here and it makes the dependency more explicit.
* `string_builder.h`: Including only `ustring.h` and `vector.h` is about as minimal as this header can get. Look elsewhere.
* `compression.h`: `Compression::decompress_dynamic()` is less commonly used than `Compression::decompress()`, and it is only accessed via a pointer here, so by forward-declaring the template `Vector`, the include to `vector.h` can be dropped. That said, all users still end up using `Vector` in other parts of their code (in fact, `Compression::decompress()` usually writes to a Vector's `ptrw()`) so it's probably not worth it. Look elsewhere.
* `node_2d.h`: Only the parent class' header (`canvas_item.h`) is included, so this is as optimal as it can get. Look elsewhere.
* `node_3d.h`: `World3D` can be forward-declared here. Only a small set of source files under `scene/3d` uses `get_world_3d()` so compile time improvements can be expected here.

Thank you for the assessment! I've got notes for two of those files:

> vector.h

`array.h` can be dropped from this file (see #111244). I think the same can be done with `vector.h`, though that might require some additional work.

> compression.h

I think `#include <zlib.h>` can be dropped from this file.

On another note: I think the 'betweenness centrality' turned out to be pretty decent at finding hub files. But since it's based on 'shortest path lengths', it really likes pointing out files that have short paths to `typedefs.h`.

On the next update, I'm going to try another algorithm. My current thinking is to calculate the 'deep cost' of each header, based on file size, for each compile unit, and then summing the parts. That should pretty closely reflect the 'absolute cost' each header is responsible for in the total compile time, and might give us a better estimate of where to look for improvement. I'll get started on that as soon as the first slew of linked PRs is merged.

I rebased after the most recent merge, and ran a new algorithm (as described above).
The new algorithm is very good at estimating how we can make the best progress on compile time, because it estimates costs from bytes parsing caused by each header.

The results indicate that system headers are quite expensive, probably because they're included in literally every file. It will be difficult to reduce this, but there are some entries in the top 100 that can probably be improved.

In the future, I'd like to explore a secondary algorithm that estimates how many recompiles each header will cause, such that we can reduce this metric separately. Both will help with development in their own ways.

> thirdparty/jolt_physics/Jolt/Core/Core.h: 463mb

This comes from needing to include `Jolt/Jolt.h` before including anything else Jolt-related, as mentioned [here](https://github.com/jrouwe/JoltPhysics/blob/9e48d59beea6a10ee8dfed45216c2dec7e9a8918/HelloWorld/HelloWorld.cpp#L6-L8).

This doesn't apply to only the integration in `modules/jolt_physics` but also (probably more importantly) our compiling of Jolt itself, which makes up a significant chunk of the full compile times currently.

In the Godot Jolt extension I relied on (like the comment there suggests) precompiled headers to mitigate the cost of this, which does have a significant impact, but since Godot didn't rely on them anywhere else I opted not to use them when porting it all over to Godot.

Most bigger C++ projects I've worked on have relied on precompiled headers in some form, but almost invariably they get brought up at some point as being either finnicky, counter-productive or a pain in the neck for other reasons. I just assumed that they had been dismissed in Godot for similar reasons, but if that's not the case then I would probably suggest looking into that, since they can reduce compile times _massively_[^1] for widely used headers that don't change often, like the standard library or third-party libraries.

As far as I'm aware they should be well-supported by all three major compilers, and have been for many years.

[^1]: So long as you're careful about managing their size, if I remember correctly, as there was some kind of tipping point where they usually ended up being detrimental instead, at least with MSVC.

Hello, I am investigating already what I can remove from Object.h because I was already planning to do stuff with it, so I already rebased a previous PR that did that.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111262

But I wanted to know if it would be safe to go ahead and change the includes where applicable or if it would compat break something somewhere.

> This comes from needing to include `Jolt/Jolt.h` before including anything else Jolt-related, as mentioned [here](https://github.com/jrouwe/JoltPhysics/blob/9e48d59beea6a10ee8dfed45216c2dec7e9a8918/HelloWorld/HelloWorld.cpp#L6-L8).

FYI, I 'hotfixed' an update that excludes thirdparty compile units from the analysis. `Jolt.h` still appears in the top 100, but not as highly as previously.

> I 'hotfixed' an update that excludes thirdparty compile units from the analysis.

I get that we're unlikely to be moving includes around in third-party libraries, but since we're in complete control of how they're compiled it would be trivial to make a bespoke header file for the more impactful libraries (like Jolt) with some set of commonly used includes for that library (e.g. `Jolt/Jolt.h` in the case of Jolt) and compile that as a precompiled header along with the library's source files specifically.

So maybe don't sweep that under the rug just yet, assuming precompiled headers aren't a non-starter to begin with of course.

I iterated further on the analysis tool.
I realized that, so far, it had been treating every include path as exclusive, since `--trace-includes` does not repeat files that have already been mentioned. This messed with my algorithm, since it attributed the cost of files only to the first deep includer.

I first tried to solve this with `-E -Id`, but that turned out to be a dud as well, since include directives (which _were_ verbose enough) are pasted verbatim, making it difficult to resolve them.
Since I did not find any other tool that pasted include hierarchies, I made a custom clang tool, which seems to do the job. While I still need to investigate the correctness of the process more thoroughly, initial results are interesting, and more realistic than previous results.

Since the tool is getting more complicated, I have dedicated a repository to it: https://github.com/Ivorforce/clang-project-profiler

I will continue to post updated results in the OP occasionally. To recap:

- **Fresh compile cost** is an estimation of the time files contribute to the total compile time of the project. It attributes its self time by 100%, and partially attributes includee times depending on how many include paths go through this file.
- **Recompile cost** is an estimation how often a file could attribute to recompiles of compile units taking place. It calculates this by the size of the files (assuming every byte has a similar chance to be churned), and attributing costs of includees same as above.

Also, a quick update on the results of the efforts so far: Looks like we had a [drop of 5% ](https://benchmarks.godotengine.org/graph/build-time/) in the total compile time! It's slow progress, but it's something :)

Went through the `*.cpp` files that included `class_db.h` and found 4 low hanging fruits. 
All others need ClassDB unfortunately. There are also no low hanging fruits in `.h` files which include `class_db.h`.

`.cpp`: 24 -> 20 files, 16.7% reduction
`.cpp` + `.h` : 61 -> 65 files, 6.1% reduction

@StarryWorm It would be much better to group those low hanging fruits in a single PR/commit. Removing an unused include from a .cpp file doesn't have a significant impact nor pose any risk, so this shouldn't be done piecemeal (which increases the churn on CI, reviewers, mergers, etc.).

Sharing this here since I believe it is relevant. @Ivorforce rightfully pointed out on #111555 that the changes would likely do nothing, and he was right. 
To check that, I made a little python tool that lists all the includes that a file has (found recursively), which means that checking the diff before and after making a change can help identify how significant of a difference it makes.

Sharing it here since I think it could be helpful for everyone working on the excessive includes. Running on something as seemingly simple as `core/core_constants.cpp` finds 89 includes for example... 

Edit: moved it to a repo https://github.com/StarryWorm/include-analysis-tools and added 2 other tools: one that counts all total transitive includes across a folder, and one that finds all files in a folder that include a given file both directly and transitively. These tools were used to produce the stats in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111567
Edit 2025/10/13: Added a new tool to the repo for descendent include tracing.

Sharing some quick tests I made: For the recompile cost, so far I've been using file size as a surrogate 'churn potential' estimator. Today I tested whether that assumption makes sense. Turns out it's not that bad! The correlation coefficient between file size and actual churn (by checking the last 6 months of git history) is 0.6. That's a pretty decent correlation! (note that I've added jitter to x values to make the plot easier to view; the actual 'churn' values are all integers) My conclusion is that I'll continue using file size to estimate churn. It's a more dynamic value than actual churn history, and easier to measure, so I'm happy this turned out to correlate so well.

If somebody wants to see what's specifically take some time in a translation unit, you can add the options while compiling it:

- _d1reportTime_ for informations on what takes time in the parsing (the first number)
- _d2cgsummary_ for informations on what takes time in the backend (the second number)

Of course, this is specific to MSVC, so it does not imply that other compilers have exactly the same bottlenecks, but maybe it can help people that are looking for some files where to improve compile times.

Little update on my [pet project to make a tool that counts transitive includes](https://github.com/StarryWorm/include-analysis-tools)

I (well, Codex) added a mode to find which headers are the most included through the codebase (transitively or not), and this is what it found (I know the values are accurate thanks to `class_db.h` being my yardstick).

I think this metric is likely the best estimator (over file size) for the recompile cost for our files, as the number of implementation files that include that given header is the number of units that will be recompiled upon modification. Whoever causes more units to be recompiled should be more expensive. 

*Note: this was run on https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111573 instead of master since it's more up-to-date on the efforts with regards to `class_db.h`.*

As needed for some evaluation on #117516, [my tool](https://github.com/StarryWorm/include-analysis-tools) can now count the total number of unique includes for each includer of a given file.

Highlighting a few things here so that everyone involved/interested in these efforts is aware:
* We have some tooling discussions on RocketChat: https://chat.godotengine.org/channel/yQRJDrPTpn5ijkZFt
  * One of those tools is @akien-mga 's `add_missing_includes` tool. Find it here: https://gist.github.com/akien-mga/c8138a5bb6154d692d475c5f14d025cf 
  * This tool can also be found in [my tools repo](https://github.com/StarryWorm/include-analysis-tools) as a python script. 
* One concern I am currently seeing and will likely be the next thing to be addressed, although it won't help with compilation times, is the use of transitively included forward-declared classes.
  * Reason: this is not IWYU-compliant; every file should include and/or forward declare what it needs, shouldn't be relying on transitive access, as it is fragile. 
* Lots of good progress has been made and keeps being made. The biggest remaining hurdle is `object.h` and `variant.h` linking to each other and creating an include overhead for pretty much the entire codebase. Progress on `GDType` may help with this, but it's TBD. 

If anyone is interested in helping with our efforts and doesn't know how to start, please do reach out either in the discussion or via DMs on RocketChat. No reduction is too small; we have over 180,000 transitive includes in the codebase, a large number of which are useless and must go.

Apologies if this has already been mentioned somewhere or is somehow not usable for Godot, but there is a tool from Google to find missing and superfluous includes: https://include-what-you-use.org/

I don't believe we ever discussed it in this proposal, but there have been lots of discussions regarding IWYU happening [in RC](https://chat.godotengine.org/channel/yQRJDrPTpn5ijkZFt), as well as steps taken towards it. 
The most significant adoption step thus far is the [use of `clangd-tidy` in our CI](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/117654), which comes with some IWYU-like behaviors, especially with regard to strictly unneeded includes. 
We haven't forced the full IWYU behavior set onto the codebase yet because of the churn it would create and the lack of highly customizable enforcement tools. There were also many issues with templates, macros, and forward declarations at the time we were discussing it, which may have been fixed in more recent releases (v0.26 and v0.27 seem to have made some progress on that front).
